references.text: Mark explains here how the Pharisees and all Jews do not eat without first washing their hands, holding fast to the tradition of the elders ([ref:Mark 7:3-4|Mark 7:3-4]). This is the same purification tradition that the water jars in Cana were intended for.
The regulations concerning cleansing with water in [ref:Lev 15:11-13|Lev 15:11-13] illustrate the Old Testament basis for the Jewish purification rituals that the six stone jars were meant to serve.

The ordinance regarding cleansing after contact with a dead body in [ref:Num 19:11-13|Num 19:11-13] is part of the Jewish law of purification that required large amounts of water—something attested by the six large stone jars.

The regulations in [ref:Lev 22:4-6|Lev 22:4-6] stating that the unclean must wash themselves with water to become clean show the need for the large quantities of water that the stone jars in Cana held.

John the Baptist's disciples discuss with a Jew about purification ([ref:John 3:25|John 3:25]). The same Greek word for "purification" (καθαρισμός) is used here as in John 2:6, linking together the theme of Jewish purification and Jesus' new work.

Many went up to Jerusalem before Passover to cleanse themselves ([ref:John 11:55|John 11:55]). This shows how central purification rituals were in Jewish practice—the same context in which the stone jars in Cana are found.

The Letter to the Hebrews refers to the old covenant's regulations about food, drink, and various washings as "external ordinances" imposed until the time of reformation ([ref:Heb 9:10|Heb 9:10]). The stone jars for Jewish purification represent exactly this old system that Jesus surpasses by turning water into wine.

The master of the banquet notes that the best wine has been saved until now ([ref:John 2:10|John 2:10]). The water in the stone jars for Jewish purification is transformed into wine—the old system is replaced by something new and better through Jesus.
